articles.title: Presidential Address: Neighborhood Effects and Missing Markets for Opportunity
articles.abstract: Experimental and quasi-experimental studies show that childhood neighborhoods have substantial causal impacts on children's adult earnings and other long-term socioeconomic outcomes. Several market failures are likely to lead to excessive residential segregation by parental income and to an undersupply of mixed-income neighborhoods. Missing markets for opportunity originate in capital market imperfections for borrowing on children's future earnings, neighbor spillovers, behavioral biases, and housing search frictions. Customized housing mobility services combined with subsidized housing vouchers can help low-income families move to higher-opportunity areas. Place-based policies that create mixed-income neighborhoods appear to increase long-term outcomes for less-advantaged children. (JEL I12, I32, I38, J13, J15, R23, R38)

articles.title: Optimal Public Transportation Networks: Evidence from the World's Largest Bus Rapid Transit System in Jakarta
articles.authors: Gabriel Kreindler, Arya Gaduh, Tilman Graff, Rema Hanna, Benjamin A. Olken
articles.abstract: Designing public transport networks involves trade-offs between coverage, service frequency, and direct service. We use the expansion of the bus system in Jakarta, Indonesia, to study these trade-offs. We analyze how new direct connections, changes in bus travel time, and wait-time reductions affect bus ridership and aggregate flows and estimate a transit network demand model by matching the route launch events. Commuters in Jakarta are 2–3 times more sensitive to wait time than bus time and inattentive to long routes. We develop a flexible framework to characterize optimal networks. A less concentrated network would increase ridership and commuter welfare. (JEL L92, L98, O18, R41, R42, R48)

articles.title: Corporate Tax Cuts, Firm Growth, and Workers' Earnings
articles.authors: Patrick J. Kennedy, Christine L. Dobridge, Paul Landefeld, Jacob Mortenson
articles.abstract: We study the effects of the largest corporate income tax cut in US history on firms and workers. To identify causal effects, we use employer-employee matched tax records and event studies comparing similarly sized firms in the same industry that faced divergent tax changes due to their preexisting legal status. Tax cuts cause increases in firms' investment, sales, profits, employment, and payrolls, with earnings gains concentrated among highly paid workers. In the short run, 87 percent of private income gains flow to the top 10 percent of the income distribution. (JEL D22, D31, G31, H25, H32, J23, L25)

articles.title: Contextually Private Mechanisms
articles.abstract: A designer employs a dynamic protocol to elicit private information. Protocols produce a set of contextual privacy violations—information learned that may be superfluous given the context. A protocol is maximally contextually private if there is no protocol that produces a proper subset of the violations it produces, while implementing the choice rule. Contextual privacy violations arise when a choice rule makes some agents collectively, but not individually, pivotal. In auctions, designing for contextual privacy requires choosing an initial question posed to each agent and the order for querying agents. Ascending-join protocols are maximally contextually private for k-item Vickrey auctions. (JEL D44, D82)

articles.title: Risk-Sharing Tests and Covariate Shocks: Drought, Floods, and Pests in Uganda
articles.abstract: Efficient risk sharing implies a simple factor structure for marginal utilities of expenditure (MUEs): Pareto weights divided by a common price. The standard approach infers MUEs from total expenditures, implicitly assuming homothetic preferences, unitary income elasticities, and identical price elasticities. Risk-sharing tests using total expenditures work for idiosyncratic shocks (budgets change, but not prices), but not “covariate” shocks (prices change). I describe all preferences that permit one to infer MUEs from expenditures and estimate nonhomothetic MUEs to test whether covariate shocks are shared efficiently in Uganda. This delivers sensible results; the standard approach suggests that droughts, floods, and pests are beneficial. (JEL D12, D81, O12, O13, Q12)

articles.title: Rationing by Race
articles.abstract: We document how deepening resource scarcity results in rationing on the basis of race in a high-stakes setting: health care. Using detailed, time stamped data on 107,000 inpatient admissions to a large health system, we find that in-hospital mortality increases for Black but not White patients as hospitals reach capacity. These findings are not explained by differential patient selection. We identify rationing by wait times as a mechanism, documenting that sicker Black patients wait longer for care than healthier White patients at almost all capacity levels. Text analysis of unstructured clinical notes reveals rationing of provider effort as another mechanism. (JEL I11, I12, I14, J15)

articles.title: Defying Distance? The Provision of Medical Services in the Digital Age
articles.abstract: Digital platforms reduce geographic frictions, enabling better matching between service providers and users. I quantify reallocation gains in Swedish online health care, using nationwide time-conditional random assignment between patients and physicians. Matching high-risk patients with doctors effective at reducing Emergency Room visits lowers such visits by 4.4 percent (SE 1.3); reallocations also reduce Counter-Guideline antibiotics by 3.1 percent (1.4). I find limited trade-offs in matching; horizontal differentiation among doctors and varied patient needs allow improvement in multiple outcomes simultaneously. Efficiency-enhancing reallocations also affect equity. The findings highlight the potential for care reorganization aligning provider heterogeneity with patient needs when geographic constraints are lifted. (JEL C78, H51, I11, I13, I14, I18)

articles.title: Intergenerational Impacts of Secondary Education: Experimental Evidence from Ghana
articles.authors: Esther Duflo, Pascaline Dupas, Elizabeth Spelke, Mark Walsh
articles.abstract: We provide experimental evidence on the intergenerational impacts of secondary education subsidies in a low-income context, leveraging a randomized controlled trial and 15-year longitudinal follow-up. Secondary school scholarships delay fertility, reduce unwanted pregnancies, and change partner selection. Under-one mortality is reduced by half. We also document cognitive development gains of 0.24 standard deviations of test scores by age five among children of female scholarship recipients. Means-tested secondary school scholarships are a high-return investment, with a conservatively estimated US$4.1 in benefits for each US$1 the policy would cost the government in the long run. (JEL H52, I12, I21, I26, J13, J16, O15)

articles.title: Manipulation-Robust Prediction
articles.authors: Daniel Björkegren, Joshua E. Blumenstock, Samsun Knight
articles.abstract: An increasing number of decisions are guided by machine learning algorithms. But when consequential decisions are encoded in algorithms, individuals may strategically alter their behavior to achieve desired outcomes. This paper develops an empirical approach that adjusts decision algorithms to anticipate manipulation. By explicitly modeling incentives to manipulate, our approach produces decision rules that are stable under manipulation, even when the rules are fully transparent. We stress-test this approach through a large field experiment in Kenya. When implemented, linear strategy-robust decision rules outperform standard linear models such as LASSO. (JEL C45, C93, D12, D91, G51, O12, O16)

articles.title: Marriage, Fertility, and Cultural Integration in Italy
articles.abstract: We study cultural integration as an equilibrium outcome of marital matching along cultural and education lines and intrahousehold investment decisions regarding fertility and cultural socialization. Our model allows us to identify cultural-ethnic-group-specific investment parameters and spousal preferences for marital matching. Structural estimates reveal a strong demand to preserve cultural identity on the part of immigrants and limited acceptance of the immigrants' cultural diversity on the part of natives. Furthermore, these estimates reveal a substantial heterogeneity of the parental value of children's education across cultures. Nonetheless, our estimates simulate substantial—though heterogeneous—cultural integration rates across immigrant groups. (JEL D13, J12, J13, J15, Z13)

articles.title: The Environmental Bias of Corporate Income Taxation
articles.authors: Luigi Iovino, Thorsten Martin, Julien Sauvagnat
articles.abstract: We study the relationship between corporate income taxation and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions in the United States. We show CO 2 -intensive firms benefit more from the tax advantage of debt and pay lower income taxes on their capital income. Building on these new facts, we provide evidence that a cut in the corporate income tax rate leads to a larger expansion of clean firms. We develop a multisector general equilibrium model that accounts for our evidence and quantify the impact of corporate tax reforms on aggregate emissions. A policy that eliminates the tax advantage of debt could reduce aggregate emissions without affecting GDP. (JEL D22, G32, H25, H32, Q52, Q54, Q58)

Are Voters Myopic or Looking for Improvement?
articles.abstract: Timing of valence outcomes plays an important role in key theories of electoral choice, and different models place different emphases on past and future outcomes. Whereas sanctioning models consider only retrospective evaluations as an accountability mechanism, selection models hold that voters use past and proposed future conditions to infer the incumbent’s ability to deliver benefits. Drawing on four surveys run on six different samples, we demonstrate that voters prefer improving conditions in both retrospection and prospection. In retrospection, this pattern is difficult to distinguish from overweighting of temporally proximate conditions, which gave rise to the notion of “the myopic voter.” Distinguishing the two processes, we find that people do not ignore early datapoints and reward improving conditions (in both retrospection and prospection). This preference for improvement does not simply reflect an uncritical heuristic for upward trends. People are not universally myopic and many genuinely value improving aggregate conditions retrospectively and prospectively.

articles.title: Measuring Partisanship and Representation in Online Congressional Communications
articles.authors: MICHAEL KISTNER, MICHAEL HESELTINE, ROBERT ALVAREZ, MAYA FITCH, LUCAS LOTHAMER, ELIZABETH SIMAS
articles.abstract: Social media and the internet have created new ways for representatives to communicate. How have members of Congress responded to these opportunities? We introduce a multi-platform dataset of congressional communications extending back to the onset of the social media era. Using computational language processing, we classify approximately 4.7 million tweets, 2.4 million Facebook posts, and 184,000 email newsletters authored by members of Congress between 2009 and 2022 based on intended purpose, and scale the partisanship of each message along a continuous left–right dimension. After validation, we demonstrate how our data can be used to study partisanship and representation in the contemporary Congress. Importantly, our data show congressional rhetoric has become more partisan and negative as social media usage has increased. We identify one potential mechanism contributing to this trend: partisanship and negativity receive inflated levels of positive engagement on social media relative to other forms of messaging like credit claiming or constituency service.

articles.title: “To Hell or to Connacht”: Expropriation, Inequality, and Local Legacies of Settler Colonialism
articles.authors: Jeremy Bowles, Gabriel Koehler-Derrick, Michael Olson
articles.abstract: Violent upheavals in landownership following conquest often change not only the concentration of land across individuals, but also the inequality of its distribution between groups. We argue that variation in landowners’ group identity has important implications for the provision of local public goods. We test this claim by studying the aftermath of the Cromwellian Settlement in seventeenth-century Ireland. Leveraging the lottery-based allocation of expropriated Catholic land to distinct groups of English Protestants, we find significant local variation in the extent of Protestant landownership. Drawing on rich original data, we find fewer local public goods in the long run in areas with more Protestant elites, with the largest reductions in goods that were either directly elite-funded or disproportionately benefited the Catholic majority. The results illustrate how conquest reshapes not just institutions but also long-run local inequalities, and highlight the distinct consequences of between-group inequality for the provision of public goods.

articles.title: Do good chat groups make good neighbors? Continuity and change of norms in neighbor relations under digital co-presence
articles.abstract: Based on interviews with urban residents in Germany and Israel, this study examines how residential instant messaging groups (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram) reshape the norms of “good neighboring”: reciprocity, distance, and speaking out. Drawing on Blokland’s public familiarity framework and Rosenblum’s theorizing of neighborly norms, we ask how digital co-presence transforms the relational conditions of neighboring and how these norms are negotiated within residential chat groups. We show that messenger groups lower the threshold for mutual support but introduce tensions through persistent mutual awareness, which are thenresolved through norm negotiation. Extending the public familiarity framework, we identify a complementary axis of performativity–discretion that manifests through norm negotiation. Residents calibrate between engagement and restraint, enacting “good enough” neighboring within the double-bounded constraints of a building and a chat group. We contribute to research on digitally mediated neighborhood communication by showing how urban dwellers achieve pragmatic coexistence through calibrated visibility.

articles.title: Getting Religion Wrong A Response to Toft’s “Getting Religion Right”
articles.authors: Nils-Christian Bormann, Lars-Erik Cederman, Manuel Vogt
articles.abstract: In a recent contribution to the Journal of Conflict Resolution , Monica Toft presents new data and analysis that suggest a rise in religious civil war, and question our findings on linguistic and religious cleavages' effect on armed conflict onset. We welcome Toft’s contribution, in particular her replication of our results, and the very well documented new dataset on civil wars. Yet we disagree with several of Toft’s specific claims and raise three larger questions about the study of religion and armed conflict. First, what is the relevant counterfactual when analyzing the religion-conflict link? Second, how useful is it to classify entire conflicts as religious? Third, what is the mechanism that links religion and conflict? Revisiting her analysis and adding new empirical evidence, we show that Toft fails to undermine our earlier results and does not find support for her own theoretical mechanism of religious outbidding in the Muslim world.

articles.title: Intermediaries and Asset Prices
articles.abstract: Intermediary asset pricing posits that financial institutions play a central role in financial markets, and that their decisions shape asset prices beyond simply reflecting the preferences of the average household. This perspective helps make sense of key empirical patterns: the excess volatility of asset prices, differences in price movements across asset classes, the cross-section of expected returns within asset classes, and specific arbitrage opportunities and price dislocations. We also review the implications of intermediary asset pricing for macroeconomic dynamics, international economics, and policy. In this approach, a primary channel of financial regulation and monetary policy is through alleviating constraints or removing risk from intermediary balance sheets during periods of stress. We highlight both existing progress and gaps for future research. (JEL E44, E52, F31, G12, G18, G21, G23)

articles.title: Refugees' Economic Integration
articles.authors: Dany Bahar, Rebecca Brough, Giovanni Peri
articles.abstract: Refugees are international migrants escaping persecution and crises whose economic success in their countries of destination is threatened by lack of access to labor and credit markets, limited information on employment opportunities, and loss of human capital and assets. In this paper we review the economic literature that analyzes and evaluates interventions designed to address these hurdles and facilitate refugees’ economic integration. We also draw important general lessons from a wide variety of these interventions and identify areas for further research. (JEL J15, J18, J24, J61, K37, K38, Z13)

articles.title: Demand, Competition, and Public Policy in the Automobile Industry
articles.abstract: We review the flourishing literature on the automobile industry since the seminal work of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995), or briefly BLP. Their work provides a structural equilibrium framework that forms a basis for conducting policy counterfactuals in several key areas of interest: competition policy and antitrust, trade policy, and taxation and environmental policy. The demand side of the “BLP framework” is micro-founded and allows for rich consumer heterogeneity to generate flexible substitution patterns between products. The supply side specifies marginal costs and accounts for imperfect competition. Our analysis focuses on two main questions. First, how has the framework been tailored to specific situations and how convincingly has it been evaluated to generate trust in the empirical findings and policy conclusions? Second, what has been learned about policy issues relevant in the automotive industry using the BLP equilibrium framework? (JEL H25, K21, L13, L22, L40, L62, Q58)

articles.title: Scoring the Behavioral Economics of Crime: Reflections on Unforgiving Places: The Unexpected Origins of American Gun Violence
articles.abstract: In Unforgiving Places Jens Ludwig makes a strong claim for the behavioral economics of crime, scoring it a knockout when pitted against conventional wisdom. Focusing on gun violence, he proposes a unifying explanation that draws on disciplines beyond economics, especially sociology, criminology, and psychology. Although the intended audience is mainly policymakers and the general public, scholars will benefit from reading Ludwig's thought-provoking book. In this essay, I evaluate the book's evidence and elaborate on the research needed to resolve unsettled hypotheses. I focus on several key issues, including linking self-control theory to cognitive processes, informal neighborhood social control, legitimacy in community policing, toxic environmental effects on cognition, the limits of administrative data, age-specific pathways of gun carrying, and the impact of social change. In the spirit of consilience that Unforgiving Places calls for, I argue that further engagement of the book's framework with these issues yields a promising research agenda. (JEL D11, D72, D90, H76, K14, K42, R23)

articles.title: Humans in the Loop: The Next Frontier in the Credibility Revolution
articles.authors: Megan T. Stevenson, Joshua B. Fischman
articles.abstract: Something is amiss in empirical economics. Despite the advances of the credibility revolution, published estimates tend to be inflated and overconfident. We argue that this stems from a weakness in the dominant econometric framework: treating the researcher like a calculator that mechanically implements the econometric method. We use several examples to show how properties of estimators change dramatically with humans in the loop. Under plausible assumptions on researcher behavior, low-power estimators such as instrumental variables exhibit high degrees of bias, even with a first-stage F-statistic of 200. Threshold testing on the first-stage F-statistic can reduce bias, contrary to Angrist and Kolesár (2024). And standard errors understate uncertainty, since they ignore variation due to researchers’ subjective choices. Ignoring the role of humans “in the research loop” can lead to highly biased and unreliable findings. Modifying econometric practices to address the human factor is a critical frontier of the credibility revolution. (JEL C12, C13, C26)

articles.title: Why Is Fertility So Low in High-Income Countries?
articles.authors: Melissa S. Kearney, Phillip B. Levine
articles.abstract: We consider why fertility has fallen in recent decades in almost all high-income countries. We begin by documenting declining total fertility and rising childlessness across cohorts, highlighting the need to focus on cohort versus period-specific fertility rates. With this motivation, we propose a conceptual model of fertility determination that augments the standard Becker model with an explicit role for social norms and cohort-specific contextual factors, including broad social and economic influences and an expanded set of consumption and lifestyle options. We posit that these forces have led to “shifting priorities,” reducing the centrality of parenthood. We then review existing empirical evidence and conclude that the decline in fertility likely reflects a complex mix of changing norms around work, parenting, gender roles, and leisure consistent with our cohort-based conceptual framework. We conclude with suggestions for future research and a brief discussion of policy implications. (JEL J13, J16, J18, J22, Z13)

articles.title: Deep Learning for Solving Economic Models
articles.abstract: The ongoing revolution in deep learning is reshaping research across many fields, including economics. Its effects are especially clear in solving dynamic economic models. These models often lack closed-form solutions, so economists have long relied on numerical methods such as value function iteration, perturbation, and projection techniques. Unfortunately, these approaches suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which makes global solutions computationally infeasible as the number of state variables increases. Deep learning offers a different approach: flexible tools that solve dynamic economic models by minimizing residuals in equilibrium conditions and that can handle high-dimensional problems. This development promises to broaden the scope of quantitative economics. I illustrate the approach using the neoclassical growth model. (JEL C45, C61, D83, O41)

articles.title: Conti-Brown, Peter, and Sean H. Vanatta. Private Finance, Public Power: A History of Bank Supervision in America
articles.abstract: Joseph R. Mason of Louisiana State University and BVA Group reviews “Private Finance, Public Power: A History of Bank Supervision in America” by Peter Conti-Brown and Sean H. Vanatta. The Econlit abstract of this book begins: “Presents a positive theory of how bank supervision works today, explaining how through experimentation, error, and the slow building of sometimes redundant, often warring institutions the American system of bank supervision came to be.”

articles.abstract: Willy C. Shih of Harvard Business School reviews “Industrial Policy for the United States: Winning the Competition for Good Jobs and High-Value Industries” by Marc Fasteau and Ian Fletcher. The Econlit abstract of this book begins: “Addresses industrial policy's underlying economic theory, its policy tools, and how these tools have been successfully and unsuccessfully deployed around the world, in the United States, and in several key industries.”

articles.abstract: David Robinson of Duke University and NBER reviews “How Progress Ends: Technology, Innovation, and the Fate of Nations” by Carl Benedikt Frey. articles.abstract: Maximilian Kasy of Department of Economics, University of Oxford reviews “The Microeconomics of Artificial Intelligence” by Joshua Gans. articles.abstract: Theodore Joyce of Baruch College, CUNY reviews “The Abortion Market: Buying and Selling Access in the Era Before Roe” by Katherine J. Parkin. Wade.”

articles.abstract: Peter Cramton of University of Maryland reviews “Failure by Design: The California Energy Crisis and the Limits of Market Planning” by Georg Riling. articles.abstract: Vicki L. Bogan of Duke University reviews “Funding White Supremacy: Federal Wealth Policies and the Modern Racial Wealth Gap” by Robert B. Williams. articles.title: Rebel party stigmatization: measuring the political price of a rebel past
articles.authors: María Ignacia Curiel, Cyrus Samii, Mateo Vásquez-Cortés
articles.abstract: The long-term electoral viability of rebel parties depends, in part, on acceptance of them as legitimate political actors. Yet civilians often punish perpetrators of past violence at the ballot box and conflict generates long-term antipathies that can impede democratic integration of former rebels. This paper offers a theoretical conceptualization of rebel party stigmatization and uses an experimental approach in Colombia, informed by interviews on the ground, to clarify the conditions under which stigmatization can be a relevant barrier for rebel parties. First, in semi-structured interviews, rebel party leaders and members uniformly claim that civilian stigmatization of the party is pervasive. Second, we design an endorsement experiment to measure rebel party stigmatization, whether the penalty is distinct from assessments based on ideology or platform, and for whom stigma is strongest. Civilians penalize policies and statements endorsed by the rebel party even when compared to endorsement by ideologically similar parties, indicative of stigmatization. Such rebel party stigmatization is especially strong among two types of citizens. First, citizens who otherwise share a similar ideology with the rebel party but rejected violence are the most stigmatizing, due to a political victimization effect. Second, citizens who did not live in communities with substantial FARC governance and presence are more stigmatizing—those who lived in rebelocracies do not penalize rebel parties but also do not support them strongly.

articles.title: Do protest bans make police repression more acceptable? Experimental evidence on the effects of legal repression from Turkey
articles.authors: Mert Arslanalp, Ulaş Erdoğdu, T Deniz Erkmen
articles.abstract: In explaining whether protest repression incites or suppresses mobilization, research on the repression–dissent nexus has underlined the importance of how the public views protests or their repression. This literature, however, generally does not differentiate between various forms of protest repression, examining primarily police violence; nor does it account for possible interactions between these various forms of repression. In this paper, emphasizing the varied and multilayered nature of repression, we posit that legal forms of repression can legitimize police repression in the eyes of the public. Using a 2 × 3 vignette survey experiment in Turkey, we find that the declaration of a protest ban prior to a protest increases public approval of subsequent police repression and more forceful forms of repression. This effect varies by protest issue, gender, and individuals' predisposition to comply with state decisions. Contrary to our expectations, however, it does not vary by the partisan identity of respondents. Using original data from an authoritarian context, this article contributes to the literature on the interplay between protest repression and public opinion by showing that legal repression operates not only through deterrence but also by generating public support for subsequent police repression.

articles.title: Ceasefires and civilian targeting in civil war
articles.abstract: Civilian suffering in civil wars regularly triggers calls for ceasefires, but do ceasefires actually stop the killing of civilians? Civilians account for a significant share of fatalities in contemporary civil wars, yet it is unclear whether and under which conditions ceasefires alleviate civilian suffering. We argue that ceasefires indeed decrease the intentional targeting of civilians by changing expectations and heightening scrutiny of belligerents’ conduct, which raises the risk of audience costs. To test this argument, we combine global ceasefire data with matching and difference in differences estimators. We find that ceasefires reduce civilian targeting on average but this effect is conditional on support by third parties. When a belligerent is backed by foreign governments, especially liberal democratic ones, restraint toward civilians increases under ceasefire. Additional analyses show that international attention to the conflict country spikes in the month a ceasefire is concluded, highlighting the importance of attentive international audiences for audience costs to materialize. These findings underscore the substantial influence external supporters can exert in enforcing norms of civilian protection and mitigating harm in civil wars.

articles.title: Do refugee camps impact hosts' security perceptions? Evidence from Africa
articles.abstract: Previous research argues that negative externalities associated with hosting refugee camps can lead to insecurity. But do hosts living in districts with refugee camps generally feel less secure than those living in districts with no camps? To investigate whether the presence or size of encamped refugee populations affect hosts' perceived safety, we utilize geographically referenced survey data from Afrobarometer alongside information on the sizes and locations of refugee camps at the district level. To account for theoretically plausible mediating effects, we also examine the influence of several dimensions of state capacity on security perceptions. We find no general effect of hosting a refugee camp on local-level security perceptions, regardless of camp population size. Rather, our results show that refugee camp hosts feel safer from violence and crime when the state's security and administrative capacity are strong, but not otherwise. Our findings help illuminate the factors that contribute to individuals' opinion formation regarding their security, demonstrating that state-building can act as a significant mediator of security perceptions in countries that host forced migrants.

articles.title: Civilian compliance and victimization in the Boko Haram insurgency
articles.abstract: How does variation in civilian compliance strategies shape wartime victimization? Across civil wars, some contested communities are displaced while others remain in place despite exposure to armed actors. Existing research explains civilian victimization primarily through armed actors' strategies, with limited attention to how civilians shape its form. I argue that civilian compliance, defined as accommodating the demands of armed actors without formally joining them, is a self-protection strategy that can reduce immediate danger but shifts civilians' exposure toward different forms of victimization. Drawing on fieldwork and a subnational comparison of two contested communities in northeastern Nigeria, I show that variation in civilian compliance shapes how armed actors interpret civilian behavior. Fragmented compliance, in which civilians selectively comply with the actor they perceive as most threatening, produces signals that rival forces interpret as support for the opposing side, prompting punitive operations and displacement. By contrast, dual compliance, in which civilians accommodate both rebels and state forces while presenting compliance as exclusive to each, creates behavioral ambiguity. Lacking clear evidence that civilians assist their rival, armed actors tolerate civilian presence and rely instead on surveillance and coercive extraction. The findings show that patterns of civilian compliance shape armed actors' use of violence, producing displacement in some communities and in situ victimization in others. By identifying civilian compliance as the behavioral signal through which armed actors infer civilian support, the article nuances existing explanations of variation in wartime victimization.

articles.title: Guardians of the regime: secret police formation in autocracies
articles.authors: Marius Mehrl, Mila Pfander, Theresa Winner, Cornelius Fritz
articles.abstract: Autocrats use secret police to stay in power, deterring and suppressing opposition to their rule. Existing research suggests that secret police succeed at this but also that they are not as ubiquitous as one may assume. We thus explore under which conditions secret police emerge in dictatorships. We develop a theoretical framework for potential predictors and apply statistical variable selection techniques to identify which of several candidate variables extracted from the literature on state security forces and authoritarian survival hold explanatory power. Our results suggest that secret police are more likely to emerge where rulers face structural, regime-external threats, such as organized anti-system mobilization and international rivals, witness successful regime-internal contestation abroad, and have sufficient material resources and personalized power to establish such organizations. This research contributes to our understanding of autocrats’ institutional choices and authoritarian politics.

Personality pairing improves human–AI collaboration
articles.abstract: Here we examine how AI agent “personalities” interact with human personalities to shape human–AI collaboration and performance. In a large-scale, preregistered randomized experiment, we paired 1,258 participants with AI agents prompted to exhibit varying levels of the Big Five personality traits. These human–AI teams produced 7,266 display ads for a real think tank, which we evaluated using 1,168 independent human raters, and a field experiment on X that generated nearly 5 million impressions. We found that human and AI personalities individually shaped ad quality and teamwork and that human–AI personality pairings directly influenced ad quality. For example, extraverted humans paired with conscientious AI produced the lowest quality ads, followed by conscientious humans paired with agreeable AI and neurotic humans paired with conscientious AI. In the field experiment, ad quality significantly influenced ad performance, measured by click-through rates and cost-per-click. Together, these results demonstrate that personality pairing can improve human–AI collaboration and performance. They also motivate future research on the complex implications of AI personalization for human–AI collaboration, teamwork, and performance.

articles.title: Cousin marriage and reduced exposure to intimate partner violence and coercive control
articles.abstract: Cousin marriage, practiced by over 10% of the world’s population, restructures kinship networks by overlapping blood and affinal ties. Theory makes competing predictions about how such kin density shapes intrahousehold conflict. “Protection” accounts posit that consanguinity aligns spouses’ interests and increases kin oversight, reducing men’s incentives and opportunities to use coercion. “Constraint” accounts, by contrast, emphasize that dense kin networks can prioritize family cohesion over women’s autonomy, potentially suppressing help-seeking and facilitating control. Here, I adjudicate between these hypotheses using data on ~36 to 46,000 women from Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, and Türkiye. Using cluster-fixed-effects models that compare women within the same Demographic and Health Survey primary sampling units and survey waves, I find that marriage to a first cousin is associated with a 2.5 percentage-point lower probability of physical intimate partner violence relative to nonconsanguineous unions (≈11% lower relative risk). Parallel reductions are observed for coercive controlling behaviors and estimates are robust to matching on observed confounders. The protective association for physical violence is stronger for patrilateral than matrilateral cousins, consistent with protection depending on kin with recognized authority over men in patrilineal systems rather than generic relatedness. In Türkiye, the association persists after adjusting for both spouses’ parental consanguinity, suggesting that it is not explained solely by family-level characteristics associated with the intergenerational practice of cousin marriage. These findings indicate that, in these settings, consanguinity is associated with lower reported violence and control.

articles.title: Leveraging generative AI for causal inference with unstructured data
articles.abstract: We introduce GenAI-Powered Inference (GPI), a statistical framework for causal inference using unstructured data, including text and images. GPI leverages open-source pretrained Generative AI (GenAI) models—such as large language models and diffusion models—not only to generate unstructured data at scale but also to extract low-dimensional representations that are guaranteed to capture their underlying structure. Applying machine learning to these representations, GPI enables estimation of causal effects while quantifying estimation uncertainty. Unlike existing approaches to representation learning, GPI does not require fine-tuning of GenAI models, making it computationally efficient and broadly accessible. We illustrate the versatility of the GPI framework through three applications: 1) estimating the effects of Chinese social media censorship while adjusting for textual confounders, 2) isolating the impact of specific image features from that of other correlated features in the same image, and 3) assessing the persuasiveness of political rhetoric. An open-source software package is available for implementing GPI.

Class of origin and voting: The activating role of volunteering during youth
articles.abstract: Differences in political participation between social classes are well documented, yet less is known about the mechanisms that may reduce these gaps. This article adopts a life-course perspective to investigate whether youth volunteering can mitigate class-based inequalities in electoral participation. Using longitudinal data from Germany, we analyse how class of origin affects voting for the newly enfranchised, how volunteering influences turnout, and how both factors interact. Our findings show that, while individuals from working-class backgrounds are less likely to vote and youth volunteering increases electoral participation for all, volunteering during youth nearly closes the participation gap linked to social origin and uplifts specifically blue-collar working-class children’s electoral participation. These results suggest that voluntary engagement in youth can serve as a “school of democracy,” reducing class-based inequalities in political participation starting at an early age, which remain persistent otherwise.

articles.title: Separating the Militants from the Moderates: Brazilian Industry and the Far-Right Bolsonarista Movement
articles.abstract: Why do some capitalists in the Global South come to firmly support far-right movements while others do not? This article explores this question by examining divisions among Brazilian industry leaders over the right-wing government of Jair Bolsonaro, from 2019 to 2023. Drawing on fieldwork and interviews with leaders in Brazil's main industrial association, the Federation of Industries of the State of São Paulo (FIESP), this article argues that distinct relations to the state and varying degrees of economic precarity led FIESP leaders to either remain staunch supporters of Bolsonaro's government or grow critical. Leaders in medium-sized firms from shrinking domestic manufacturing sectors decried their exclusion from policymaking under previous administrations and became some of Bolsonaro's most ardent backers. In contrast, while initially supportive of Bolsonarismo , many leaders from more competitive, internationalized sectors dominated by large firms grew critical of Bolsonaro, particularly following his chaotic response to the COVID-19 pandemic. These moderate leaders recognized the structural power they leverage over state actors, while prioritizing gradual reform and a stable political environment. In this way, different relations to state actors led to a politics of moderation or militance. The article concludes by arguing how the political rationalities tying capital to the state shape intraclass cleavages and business’ response to emergent far-right movements.

articles.title: Toward a Gender Sensitive and Locally Rooted co‐Production Approach: Insights From Implementing Child Stunting Eradication Program in Indonesia
articles.authors: Sulikah Asmorowati, Violeta Schubert, Mary S. Mangai, Jusuf Irianto, Tri Yuniningsih, Saskia Intandivanty Kamalia Anggika, Wilujeng Dwi Windhiari
articles.abstract: Co‐production is a complex and nuanced field of social action that operates at multiple levels of the policy cycle, closely interconnecting the roles, motivations, and outcomes of different social actors. But how co‐production practices are shaped by gender is often overlooked. This article highlights the complexity of co‐production practices within Indonesia's ambitious national strategy to reduce child stunting. Based on qualitative research of three local government areas implementing stunting intervention programs, we draw on the ‘Four Co(s)’ framework to explore variations across co‐commissioning, co‐design, co‐delivery, and co‐assessment. Ongoing challenges to the eradication of stunting in some areas highlight the tense intersections between early marriage, poverty and rural and technological disadvantage. But as we argue, it is also dependent on social actors, especially women, who serve as catalysts. Future research that pays closer attention to the inherently gendered expressions of co‐production is both theoretically and practically necessary.

articles.title: Coordination Costs and Homelessness Housing Form Choice
articles.authors: Edmund Poku Adu, Julius A. Nukpezah
articles.abstract: Local implementers have discretion in selecting forms of housing for the homeless, yet the determinants of these choices remain poorly understood. Using the institutional collective action (ICA) framework, this study examines California's Homekey program to assess how coordination demands shape decisions among hotel conversions, multifamily acquisitions, and modular or new construction. Drawing on binary logistic, generalized estimating equation (GEE), and multinomial logistic models, we find that larger projects and those designated as permanent housing are significantly more likely to pursue hotel conversions. Housing authorities—owing to their specialized missions and lower form‐specific coordination costs—are over six times more likely than cities to select multifamily acquisition. Local vacancy constraints further steer implementers away from modular or new construction and toward hotel conversions. These results demonstrate that implementation form is not a neutral technical decision but an institutional response to coordination challenges embedded in intergovernmental and interorganizational contexts.

articles.title: The Role of Public Administrators in Building a Robust Liberal Democracy
articles.abstract: After decades of expansion, liberal democracy is threatened by autocratic populists. These actors exploit widening gaps between leaders and citizens, as well as growing political polarization in the population, to consolidate executive power by undermining courts, sidelining elected assemblies, discrediting public administrators, and intimidating both opposition and the press. This alarming predicament begs the question of what enterprising role public administrators can play in curbing the rise of autocratic populism by reconnecting elected politicians with diverse and polarized population groups while fostering alignment among them. To this end, public administrators are conceptualized as bridgebuilders promoting interactive political leadership along the vertical axis of the political system; as mediators fostering agreement, accommodation, or compromise between polarized groups along the horizontal axis; and as institutional architects linking representative democracy and collaborative governance arenas. This expanded role of public administrators as democratic guardians and protagonists raises important questions regarding its legitimacy.

articles.title: Increasing Equitable Access in Public Service: A Descriptive Study About Accessible Materials
articles.abstract: As the digital footprint of public service expands, the need for accessible materials for individuals with disabilities grows. Public servants must consider accessibility in the creation of all materials, from websites to PDFs to audio and visual media. However, research around accessible material creation in public service has been limited. This study uses data from a 2024 survey of MPA alumni from five universities to identify their familiarity with accessible material creation, including their awareness of their own organization's policies, processes, and training. The findings reveal that respondent awareness of their own organization's practices was correlated with higher familiarity in generating accessible materials. However, many respondents did not know about their organization's practices, identifying the need for increased dialogue about this essential element of social equity and inclusion. As such, suggestions for organizations to improve their practices around accessible material creation along with ideas for continued research are shared.

articles.title: The Practice and Origins of Performance Measurement: Assessing the Sunnyvale Model, 1984–2023
articles.authors: Joyce Kasing Tagal, Derek Ouyang, Daniel E. Ho
articles.abstract: Few regulatory reforms are as celebrated or emulated as the performance measurement system of Sunnyvale, California, which inspired the Government Performance and Results Act of 1993 and countless other national and local efforts. This study presents the first longitudinal, cross‐programmatic analysis of a performance measurement system, introducing a digital archival approach to analyze 152 performance indicators across 35,000 pages of documents from 1984 to 2023, supplemented with interviews of key stakeholders. Even if Sunnyvale's system initially functioned as an exemplar of performance‐based decision‐making, it deteriorated with weakened commitment and, more importantly, sustained significant implementation costs while its benefits reduced over time. The findings illustrate three core trade‐offs for performance measurement systems: measuring what matters (the “quantity‐quality” tradeoff); ensuring continuity while allowing for adaptation (the “continuity‐flexibility” tradeoff); and ensuring accountability without having implementation detract from productivity (the “accountability‐productivity” tradeoff).

articles.title: Public Employee Pensions and Municipal Insolvency
articles.abstract: This paper studies how municipal governments jointly manage spending, credit market borrowing, and a public employee pension system. I model governments as levered investors who must meet non-defaultable pension obligations and may value government spending more than citizens. I quantify the model using data on California cities, including a new record of fiscal emergencies, tax increases required to maintain essential city services. After the financial crisis depleted pension funds, cities engaged in excessive risk-taking: the fiscal emergency option encouraged gambling for resurrection that kept cities vulnerable to shocks well into the recovery. To correct this problem, a savings requirement works better than a restriction on risk-taking or a pension funding requirement. The policy experiments emphasize that effective policies need to target the combined pension and bond finances, as policies that only target one, such as a pension funding requirement, are undermined by endogenous changes to the other.

articles.title: Equity Frictions and Firm Ownership
articles.abstract: In this paper, I document systematic heterogeneity in ownership and financing of firms across Eurozone countries. To rationalize these differences, I build a quantitative general equilibrium model of workers and entrepreneurs who choose debt and equity financing of their firms, subject to rich country-specific financial frictions. The novel data on firm ownership and financing, combined with the structure of the model, allows me to quantify the level of debt and equity frictions in each country. Quantitatively, I find much larger output effects from equity frictions: harmonizing them across countries would lead to nearly four times larger output effects compared to debt frictions, and removing them would increase aggregate output by 73\% more. The larger impact on output is due not only to the estimated levels and dispersion of equity frictions but also to the greater risk sharing provided by equity, which further incentivizes entrepreneurs to expand their firms. Through their effect on risk sharing, equity frictions also rationalize the observed negative relationship between equity financing and wealth inequality. Quantitatively, they are responsible for over 70\% of the explained variation in top wealth shares across countries.

articles.title: (Un)intended consequences of mass-prescribing GLP-1s
articles.authors: Luc L. Hagenaars, Laura A. Schmidt
articles.abstract: It is difficult to overstate how much glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) pharmacotherapies have inundated the public discourse on obesity. An avalanche of scientific papers, news articles, and social media posts debate the efficacy, affordability, and appropriateness of GLP-1 receptor agonists not just for obesity but also skin disease, erectile dysfunction, pregnancy, and addiction. Attempting to cut through the noise, the World Health Organization (WHO) recently published the first-ever global guidelines recommending GLP-1s for the treatment of obesity, while committing to develop a global framework ensuring “fair access” to these medicines for the 1 billion people affected worldwide. Going deeper, the guidelines also advocate for “robust populationlevel policies” to address the root causes of obesity in unhealthy food environments. However, to complicate these efforts, WHO’s recommendations unfold at a time rife with competitive pressures among pharmaceutical companies, food companies vying for the GLP-1 market segment, and wellness companies promoting supplements and telemedicine programs for what is being billed as a GLP-1 lifestyle. This commercial milieu is ripe for unintended consequences that conspire against fair access to these medicines.

articles.title: Context disadvantage and residential mobility from early life into adulthood: impacts on socio-economic outcomes
articles.authors: Sergi Vidal, Maël Lecoursonnais, Riccardo Valente, Maria Brandén
articles.abstract: Individuals’ socio-economic trajectories are shaped by both persistence and change in their residential environments, making it essential to examine how the socio-spatial dynamics of context disadvantage and residential mobility interact over the life course. While prior research has often studied these factors separately and within specific life stages, less is known about their compound effects and their interrelatedness across childhood and adulthood. This study addresses this gap by investigating how exposure to residential contexts and residential mobility from birth influences socio-economic outcomes in early adulthood. Using Swedish longitudinal register data, we analyze residential trajectories and their association with economic and occupational (dis) advantage among individuals born between 1990 and 1993. Our findings show that mobility magnifies the associations between context exposure and socio-economic outcomes. Prolonged exposure to disadvantaged areas is most harmful when it coincides with moving, consistent with a compound penalty of instability and resource-poor environments. Second, moves in childhood are generally detrimental, while adult moves are opportunity-enhancing unless they occur in disadvantaged contexts, where the mobility premium levels off. Third, exiting disadvantaged contexts is associated with higher attainment than remaining persistently exposed, indicating that later socio-spatial trajectories can attenuate earlier disadvantage. These findings underscore the importance of considering both residential context and mobility across the life course for understanding—and interrupting—the reproduction of socio-economic inequality.

articles.title: One overworking breadwinner or two earners? Family economic standard of living by breadwinner arrangement, 1960 to 2018–2022
articles.abstract: Has the rise of rewards to long and inflexible work schedules altered the household-level economic viability of gendered divisions of paid work within marriage? This paper examines whether household arrangements centered on an overworking single breadwinner have become increasingly competitive, in terms of family economic standard of living, with non-overworking dual-breadwinner households. As prior research documents increasing rewards to overwork, particularly in professional and managerial occupations, overworking single-breadwinner families may have become economically competitive with dual-breadwinner households in which neither partner overworks. Using decennial Census and American Community Survey data from the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series covering 1960 to 2018–2022, we compare breadwinner arrangements across the income distribution and decompose changes in family income into changes in men’s earnings, women’s earnings, and non-labor income. Results show that overworking male- and female-breadwinner families experienced substantial relative gains at the top of the income distribution. Decomposition analyses indicate that these gains were driven primarily by accelerated earnings growth among overworking single breadwinners rather than earnings stagnation among dual earners. Although dual-breadwinner families with overworking breadwinners remain the most advantaged group, the gap between them and overworking single-breadwinner families narrowed substantially by 2018–2022. These findings suggest that labor market reward structures associated with long and inflexible work schedules may reshape family-level economic incentives in ways that reinforce gendered divisions of paid work, particularly among affluent families.

The territorial rights of wild animals: Justification
articles.abstract: Territorial rights (TR) have become foundational in normative political theory, addressing pressing questions about boundary drawing, governance, and resource use. Influential TR theorists Cara Nine and Margaret Moore justify humans’ TR based on the functional, social, and identity‐anchored normative significance of non‐substitutable places. However, these arguments treat animals as resources, excluding them from normative consideration and political standing. This article analyzes Nine and Moore's arguments to assess whether their justificatory logic applies to wild animals. Using mule deers as a case study, I test whether they have sufficiently weighty interests in occupancy, residency, resource use, and control to ground duties on humans and whether TR theories should continue to treat animals as mere natural resources.

articles.title: Sex, Romance, or Recreation? An Experiment Testing the Effects of Cannabis Brand-generated Social Media Ads on College Students’ Expectancies and Intentions to Use Cannabis Prior to Sex
articles.authors: Jessica Fitts Willoughby, Stacey J. T. Hust, Leticia Couto, Jiayu Li, Soojung Kang
articles.abstract: Sexual and romantic scripts are used to market cannabis products, now legal for adult-use in several U.S. states. We conducted an online experiment ( N = 747) examining the impact of viewing brand-generated social media posts promoting cannabis that included sexual, romantic, and non-sexual non-romantic recreational scripts among college students in Washington state. Increased perceptions that ads suggested cannabis enhances sex were associated with higher sex-related cannabis expectancies. Among men, wishful identification was associated with lower sexual risk expectancies among those who viewed sexual scripts and a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex among those who viewed sexual or romantic scripts. Among women, perceiving that ads suggested cannabis enhances sex was associated with a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex, whereas perceiving that ads suggested cannabis impacts sexual consent was associated with a lower likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex. Additionally, wishful identification among women was associated with a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex. Findings highlight associations between perceptions of brand-generated social media posts, expectancies, and intentions to use cannabis before sex among college students and identify mechanisms through which effects may occur.

articles.title: Experimental Research on Stereotype Expression in Freely Generated Language: A Systematic Literature Review
articles.authors: Kim T. Beenen, Camiel J. Beukeboom, Christian Burgers, Pia Sommerauer
articles.abstract: Social stereotypes spread through biased language. Experiments in which participants freely generate language allow researchers to causally test how stereotypes affect language use and capture multiple linguistic variables simultaneously, offering high ecological validity. Despite this potential, it remains unclear how and to which extent this paradigm has been used to study linguistic biases. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review ( k = 106 experiments) and found that most freely generated language experiments examined only one linguistic variable, leaving the interplay between linguistic variables largely underexplored. To advance our understanding of stereotype expression in everyday language, we recommend experiments to measure multiple linguistic variables simultaneously and in relation to each other. This knowledge is needed to address harmful stereotype communication in the real world through automated detection tools, communication interventions, and the fine-tuning of Large Language Models.

articles.title: Investigating Conditional Macro-Level Media Effects Over a Long-Term: How Crisis Periods Moderate the Effects of Suicide Coverage on Suicide Rate Change (1861–2007)
articles.authors: Christina Viehmann, Stefan Geiß, Manina Biermayer, Oliver Quiring, Florian Arendt
articles.abstract: How does media shape society over decades, and does its effect vary depending on the societal atmosphere or zeitgeist ? While theoretically important, there is a lack of systematic empirical evidence on conditional long-term macro-level media effects. We propose a broader framework to study such effects and demonstrate its applicability for the “Werther effect” in the UK. More specifically, we investigate whether media coverage of suicides in a newspaper of record is linked to suicide rates and whether this link changes during societal crises. For this, we combine suicide data with a large-scale automated content analysis of crisis and suicide reporting in The Times over a century (1861-2007). Our analysis shows that increased suicide reporting is associated with higher suicide rates, but only during crisis periods. The results are consistent with a conditional Werther effect and may offer one piece of the larger puzzle of long-term macro-level media influences on society.

Conditional Autonomy, Discursive Gatekeeping, and Patterns of Action: How Experts Influence Policy in China's One‐Party System
articles.abstract: This paper examines how experts exert influence within China's one‐party system, where policymaking is ideologically disciplined and knowledge‐intensive. It combines the Functional Theory of Agency, which identifies patterns of action including accumulation of knowledge, brokerage, entrepreneurship, and leadership, with a typology of four expert configurations—near‐power, academic, market‐oriented, and Societal experts—to explain differences in institutional embeddedness and resource base. The paper argues that these configurations operate under conditions of conditional autonomy; expert influence becomes possible through alignment with the dominant discursive, temporal and institutional order of the Party‐state. Discursive gatekeeping determines which forms of expert agency become feasible and consequential under specific political conditions. This argument is illustrated using Caoyang New Village renewal project in Shanghai, a high‐salience planning case where discursive framing, safety and stability boundaries, and political timing activate and constrain expert roles. Near‐power experts perform leadership and intra‐bureau brokerage, while academic experts broker and selectively pursue entrepreneurship. Market‐oriented experts advance entrepreneurship and project‐level leadership, while Societal experts engage in brokerage and collective leadership, pursuing micro‐entrepreneurship within tacitly tolerated boundaries. The paper's contribution is to demonstrate that political control does not merely suppress expertise but differentiates and organizes expert agency into distinct, policy‐relevant forms.

articles.title: Disclosing Power Dynamics in Metropolitan Governance: An Analysis of Network Micro‐Mechanisms of Change in an Evolving Inter‐Municipal Network
articles.authors: Karina Arias‐Yurisch, Karina Retamal‐Soto, Alejandro Espinosa‐Rada
articles.abstract: This study investigates power dynamics in metropolitan governance by analyzing the evolution of an inter‐municipal network in a Latin American city. It argues that actors build partnering strategies in a bid to improve their position in the network while minimizing the costs of collaborative action. These network micro‐mechanisms aggregate to produce macro‐level structures that may or may not mitigate the starting power asymmetries. By applying stochastic actor‐oriented models (SAOMs) to longitudinal data for 2009–2021, corresponding to three mayoral terms, the research reveals how collaborative dynamics are driven by resource disparities and preferential attachment that, in turn, reinforce the central positions of certain municipalities and potentially exacerbate power imbalances in metropolitan governance. The findings underscore the critical importance of considering these power dynamics when studying the operation and performance of polycentric governance systems, particularly in contexts marked by existing inequalities.

articles.title: From Policy Legitimization to Blame Avoidance—Discursive Strategies During Denmark's Mink Culling Crisis
articles.authors: Olivier Rubin, Olov Hemmingsson, Evangelia Petridou, Jörgen Sparf
articles.abstract: This paper examines how governments navigate policy legitimacy during crises through three distinct discursive processes: legitimization, delegitimization, and blame avoidance. Using a sequential mixed‐methods design, the study analyzes Denmark's decision to cull all mink during the COVID‐19 pandemic. The quantitative analysis of 947 newspaper articles indicates that while both periods were characterized by negative coverage, the force and target of delegitimization discourses shifted dramatically from questioning policy outcomes to scrutinizing procedural legitimacy. The qualitative analysis illustrates how, initially, the government successfully legitimized the mink culling through appeals to scientific authority, with broad political and public support. However, following legal and scientific challenges, policy legitimacy collapsed, coinciding with a strategic pivot from policy justification to blame avoidance. The analysis illustrates that legitimization and blame avoidance can be treated as analytically distinct discursive strategies: legitimization proactively affirms policy necessity through evidence and legal appeals, while blame avoidance reactively deflects responsibility through reframing, buck‐passing, and scapegoating. The policy persisted despite sustained delegitimization, initially aided by legitimization efforts and later by blame avoidance strategies. The findings advance policy theory by clarifying how discursive strategies evolve across a policy's lifecycle and offer a framework applicable to other high‐salience domains such as climate emergencies and migration policies.

articles.title: Cool Citizens? How Affectively Unpolarized Citizens View and Participate in Democracy
articles.authors: Peter Luca Versteegen, Joseph B. Phillips, Lilliana Mason
articles.abstract: Does affective polarization change how citizens view and participate in democracy? We posit that the answer to this crucial question depends on how affectively un polarized citizens view and participate in democracy. Yet, the most common operationalization of affective polarization––measuring sympathy ratings for one party relative to another––does not differentiate between people’s absolute sympathy ratings for the parties, which may mask essential heterogeneity among unpolarized citizens. This paper theorizes the methodological origin of this heterogeneity, describes it, and highlights its implications. Cluster analyses and regressions from three nationally representative surveys in the US provide three conclusions. First, substantial shares of the US population are affectively un polarized. Second, unpolarized citizens cluster into two groups: one feeling lukewarm and one feeling cold toward both parties. Third, these unpolarized groups report diverging democratic attitudes and participation patterns. We discuss the methodological implications and the need for future research on affectively unpolarized citizens.

articles.title: Women Politicians’ Role Model Effects: The Influence of Shared Identities Beyond Gender
articles.abstract: Women consistently report lower levels of political interest and political ambition than men. Studies have examined how women politicians as role models can make women more politically engaged, but studies have not typically examined additional shared identities beyond gender. I propose that women politicians with whom women share additional identities will be perceived as more relatable and inspiring and, consequently, have stronger role model effects on women’s political engagement. Through a conjoint experiment (Study 1), I find that having additional shared identities with a woman politician increases perceptions of her as relatable and inspiring. However, a survey experiment with novel video treatments depicting a woman politician’s story (Study 2) did not produce positive role model effects on women’s political interest, internal political efficacy, or nascent political ambition – regardless of additional shared racial and partisan identity with the woman politician. Moreover, the video treatment had remarkably different effects across White and Black women, regardless of additional shared racial and partisan identity. An observational analysis (Study 3) replicates the finding that additional shared racial and partisan identity with women political representatives is not systematically correlated with higher levels of political interest. These findings carry important implications for understanding women politicians’ role model effects and the potential of role models to increase women’s political engagement.

articles.title: Social Class and Forced Migrants’ Secondary/Onward Mobility Decision-Making: Syrians in Turkey and Lebanon
articles.abstract: This article aims first to understand how and why refugees decide to leave or stay in their first country of asylum, and second to contribute to the theory of agentic analyses of migration. Our contribution adds to the growing body of research examining the impact of social class and associated capitals on the trajectories of forced migrants. Our analysis of the experiences of Syrians in Turkey and Lebanon demonstrates that social class is a critical factor in shaping their experiences in their first countries of asylum. We assert that social class has a significant impact on their future mobility and immobility decisions. By using a Bourdieusian conceptualisation of capitals, habitus and social space and relying on in-depth interviews, we analyse the types of capital that forced migrants possess, their convertibility and their chances of re-establishing their class status. We show that convertibility depends on the type of capital and its interaction with social space. The difference between pre- and post-displacement class status is a significant factor in determining decisions regarding onward mobility, along with the capacity for social reproduction. Our findings demonstrate that voluntary immobility may occur among those who have achieved similar livelihoods to their pre-displacement status and are content with their lives. Lower-income households that struggle to restore their livelihoods are more likely to engage in irregular migration or become trapped in involuntary immobility.

articles.title: The Societal Determinants of Climate Risk for Refugees: Evidence From Global and African Refugee Corridors
articles.abstract: While a growing body of research examines the relationship between climate change and displacement in origin communities, less is known about the climate risks that displaced populations encounter in host areas. This study examines how climate risk (disaggregated into hazard exposure, vulnerability, and coping capacity) is reconfigured as refugees move from origin to host countries. We argue that the societal determinants of climate risk—in this analysis, the structural and institutional conditions of host and origin countries that mediate the consequences of hazard exposure—are at least as consequential as hazard exposure in shaping the climate risk environments in which displaced populations live. Drawing on the Climate-driven INFORM Risk Index and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Population Statistics from 2013 to 2022, we apply a migration corridor analysis globally and within Africa. We find a global rise in the number of refugees originating from high climate risk countries, and that 75 percent of global refugees reside in high or medium climate risk host countries. In Africa, displacement to neighboring or regional host countries shifts exposure to hazards but often not overall climate risk. as many refugees remain in countries characterized by high societal vulnerability and low coping capacity. Refugees who move intercontinentally typically face lower climate risks. Our findings demonstrate that cross-border displacement often reconfigures rather than alleviates climate risk, as the societal conditions that produce vulnerability prove far more persistent than patterns of hazard exposure.

articles.title: Estimating the influence of learning disabilities on educational attainment: a sibling comparison analysis with a gender perspective
articles.abstract: This study investigated the longitudinal relationship between learning disabilities (LD) in adolescence and educational attainment, as well as the underlying mechanisms behind this relationship. Using a sibling sample from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (N = 1,710), this study employed sibling fixed effects models to account for unobserved family-level characteristics such as genes and early childhood family and social context. Sobel mediation analyses were performed on a gender-stratified sample to investigate the following mechanisms: educational aspirations and expectations, educational effort, and school-based relationships. Sibling fixed effects estimates revealed that LD in adolescence was negatively associated with years of schooling completed in adulthood (b = −0.494, P &lt; 0.01). Gender-stratified models showed that only the association for girls was statistically significant (b = −0.689, P &lt; 0.05). Among girls, this association was partially explained by a combination of educational aspirations and expectations, educational effort, and school-based relationships, with educational aspirations and expectations being the most salient mechanism. These findings highlight that LD is not only an individual cognitive designation but also a socially mediated experience with long-term educational consequences, especially for girls. Policymakers and practitioners may consider developing and implementing interventions that address both educational and social challenges faced by girls with LD.

articles.title: Get out to deliberate (GOTD): Door-to-door canvassing to improve civic engagement
articles.authors: Katy Tabero, Zohreh Khoban, Paolo Spada, Rafael Mestre, Matt Ryan
articles.abstract: Several decades of experimentation have found that ‘Get-Out-the-Vote’ (GOTV) campaigns can effectively increase voter turnout. Yet, little has been said about the ability of similar-style campaigns to encourage participation in other types of civic engagement, such as citizens’ assemblies, which require much higher levels of commitment. Furthermore, although studies have found general support for citizens’ assemblies, willingness to participate is higher amongst those already more politically engaged and with higher levels of education, presenting a challenge to claims surrounding legitimacy and representation. In this article, we conduct a GOTV-style field experiment, complemented by a doorstep survey, to increase and understand perspectives towards registration for the 2023 Southampton Citizens’ Climate Assembly. We find that canvassing can be an effective method for increasing registration, including from under-represented groups. However, there are considerable barriers to participation, particularly the level of commitment, personal interest, and concerns about impact, which limit recruitment efforts.

articles.title: The rhetoric of responsibility in party manifestos (1980–2021)
articles.abstract: Focusing on the responsibility–responsiveness dilemma, we analyze responsibility rhetoric (defined as the emphasis on elements such as national solidarity, the public interest, and public-spiritedness), hypothesizing that it is used by parties moderating their policy positions, to justify deviations from their traditional standpoints, as well as by large incumbent parties seeking to claim credit for their responsible actions. In contrast, populist and niche parties, which prioritize responsiveness, are expected to avoid such rhetoric. We apply the manifestoberta Large Language Model (LLM) to classify natural sentences from up to 1,927 party manifestos (1980–2021), covering 38 countries worldwide, into the traditional MARPOR/Comparative Manifesto Project (CMP) coding categories. We then adopt two methods, a semisupervised Latent Dirichlet allocation topic model (Seeded-LDA) and the OpenAI GPT-4o-mini LLM, to refine one of these categories by selecting only those sentences that align with our concept of responsibility rhetoric. The results of statistical analysis support our hypotheses and are robust across different operationalizations of the dependent variable.

articles.title: Congressional Oversight Reports as Legislative Branch Work Product and Research Resource
articles.authors: Grace A. Moore, David Rapallo, Sean M. Theriault
articles.abstract: The Levin Center for Oversight and Democracy at Wayne State University Law School is in the process of creating the first‐ever comprehensive database of congressional oversight reports for all House and Senate Committees since the 106th Congress (1999–2000). In this article, we place these reports into the broader context of the tools Congress has to conduct oversight in service of its many legislative branch responsibilities under the Constitution. We also explain the development of the database. We conclude the article by discussing how the congressional scholars in this special issue use this database to examine how Congress conducts oversight, and we propose several additional areas for future study.

articles.title: Social Norms, State Punishment, and Motivation Crowding in Anti‐Corruption Messaging: Experimental Evidence From China
articles.abstract: A growing body of scholarship views corruption not merely as a failure of monitoring and enforcement but as a resilient informal institution sustained by social perceptions—and misperceptions. When citizens believe others tolerate or engage in corruption, resisting it becomes a collective action problem, allowing corruption to perpetuate itself. Using a large‐scale survey experiment in China, this study tests whether correcting exaggerated perceptions of social tolerance for corruption can help break this cycle. We find that providing information about the actual (low) level of tolerance significantly strengthens anti‐corruption attitudes and intentions, especially among those who mistakenly believed a majority tolerated corruption. However, this effect is weakened when paired with punishment cues, suggesting that enforcement information can crowd out the motivational force of norm‐based messages. Our findings demonstrate both the potential and the limits of norm‐based informational interventions and offer implications for anti‐corruption messaging in comparable contexts.

articles.title: Why Some Critical Junctures Lead Nowhere: Exploring Dynamic and Static Policy Paths
articles.abstract: Some critical junctures fail to cause significant change in practice. Inspired by historical institutionalism, this article develops the concept of dynamic and static policy paths to explain why some critical junctures do not lead to change, while others do. Combining insights from policy process literature and policy implementation, it conceptualizes critical junctures through four elements: framing, targets, instruments, and actors/institutions. Based on two case studies, the article argues that the importance of framing and targets has been overexaggerated, and that a dynamic path will not occur unless there is also a significant change in instruments and actors/institutions. In Denmark, a climate policy agreement created a new policy direction for agriculture in which climate policy is a key component. In Norway, a climate policy agreement did not change the trajectory of sectoral policy and climate policy development has remained stagnant. Thus, differences in the critical junctures led to different policy paths.
