Where Are the Most Influential Articles in Political Science Published?
articles.abstract: Where are the most influential articles in political science published? Drawing on citation data from the Web of Science, this article identifies the most-cited political science journal articles each decade from the 1940s through the 2020s. The results depict a changing discipline: the American Political Science Review still leads the field, but its once-dominant position has attenuated as a wider range of journals have become homes for highly cited work. Methodological papers now account for a substantial share of the discipline’s most influential research, reflecting the growing centrality of technical innovation.

articles.title: Delegating Away Democracy? Martial Law Support in South Korea
articles.abstract: Why do citizens sometimes accept undemocratic actions by political leaders? Building on growing debates about citizens’ democratic attitudes, we examine whether support for executive power grabs is associated not only with citizens’ partisan alignment but also with their perceptions of government performance and animosity toward political opponents. South Korea’s sudden declaration of martial law in December 2024 offers a unique real-world case for examining this question. Using original survey data collected 1 month after the incident from 1,500 respondents, we find that individuals with positive views of the economy, particularly incumbent supporters, are more likely to endorse the stated justifications for martial law. Hostility toward the opposition is also associated with higher endorsement among incumbent supporters and with a weaker observed relationship between economic evaluations and democratic accountability. Our findings suggest that even in established democracies, public support for democratic norms may be fragile in times of crisis—especially under deep polarization and when citizens view the executive as effective.

articles.title: Context, script, cue: understanding human–AI intimate relationships
articles.authors: Fan Yang, Meiling Du, Ningxin Li, Qing Yan
articles.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the intimate sphere of human relationships presents a profound challenge to traditional understanding of intimacy, necessitating a critical examination of this technology’s extension into a domain that has always been viewed as deeply human. Through in-depth semi-structured interviews (N = 23), this study examines how human–AI intimate relationships develop in Chinese society at the intersection of traditions and modernization. A three-pronged Context-Script-Cue (CSC) framework emerges, capturing how users navigate emotional investment alongside the artificial nature of AI. By empirically examining how users engage in human–AI intimate relationships, this study offers the new CSC framework for understanding the development of human–AI intimate relationships.

articles.title: A comparative test of the protection motivation theory: active and passive privacy protection in Brazil, Germany, the United States, and Vietnam
articles.authors: Yannic Meier, Laurent H Wang, Nicole C Krämer, Miriam J Metzger
articles.abstract: Online companies surveil users around the world for commercial purposes. We advance protection motivation theory (PMT), by categorizing user responses to surveillance as either active or passive (i.e., self-inhibition) privacy protection behavior, integrating privacy literacy overconfidence, and exploring privacy resignation as a moderator. Finally, we adopt a comparative lens by investigating protection behavior in four national contexts: Brazil, Germany, the United States, and Vietnam. Results of an online survey (Ntotal = 2,092) show that perceiving surveillance as privacy threat was not consistently associated with active protection behavior. Rather, self-inhibition was a more likely response to surveillance which may have detrimental consequences for both individuals and societies. Across countries, perceived effectiveness of active protection positively relates to both forms of protection while active protection does not prevent self-inhibition. Interestingly, privacy resignation may not always impede protection. In summary, not all aspects of PMT are generalizable when using a culturally diverse sample.

Community-minded communists: A field experiment on party member propensity for community activism in rural Vietnam
articles.authors: Paul Schuler, Eitan Paul, Quynh Nguyen, Markus Taussig, Mai Truong
articles.abstract: In single-party and dominant-party regimes, do party members and non-party members at the grassroots level respond differently to party-linked collective action? This paper examines how different framings of party-linked collective action shape participation among party members and non-party members in Vietnam – one of the world’s most enduring single-party regimes – using a preregistered field experiment involving more than 7000 rural women. Contrary to assumptions that party members engage in party-linked collective action for selective or ideological reasons, we find that party members are also more responsive to collective, community-oriented framings. Using a field experiment and interviews, we show that grassroots party members are more community-minded than their non-party counterparts. These findings suggest that, in addition to careerism or ideological loyalty in authoritarian party membership, altruistic and community-minded engagement is an important additional dimension. The presence of community-oriented grassroots party members has important implications for the legitimacy and durability of dominant-party regimes.

articles.title: Re-electing the party leader: The 2024 PASOK contest
articles.abstract: This article examines leadership contests in European mainstream parties confronting electoral decline and attempting to restore competitiveness. Focusing on this broader phenomenon, it analyses incumbent leaders seeking renewed mandates through open primary elections in such contexts. The article applies Stark’s (1996) selection criteria (‘acceptability’, ‘electability’ and ‘competence’) to the 2024 Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) leadership contest in Greece as a demanding empirical and methodological setting: an incumbent leader seeking re-election through a competitive open primary within a recovery major party after only limited electoral improvement. Drawing on candidates’ speeches, press reports, official results and polling indicators mapped onto Stark’s criteria, the study evaluates party members’ and supporters’ perceptions of the main contenders. The findings show that the incumbent leader, Nikos Androulakis, led his opponents on all three criteria and suggest that incumbent re-election in recovery major parties is broadly consistent with Stark’s model when electability is interpreted as credible electoral recovery and unity concerns stem from strategic rather than ideological conflict.

articles.title: How preferential voting and party ideology shape campaign-focus in proportional electoral systems
articles.authors: Julius Lehtinen, Mikko Mattila, Åsa von Schoultz
articles.abstract: While electoral systems shape candidates’ incentives to cultivate personal reputations, institutional rules do not translate mechanically into campaign behaviour. We argue that both electoral institutions and ideological traditions shape campaign strategies: ideological traditions influence both the attractiveness of candidate-centred appeals and how strongly candidates respond to institutional incentives. We present the first large cross-national test of their joint influence, using data from 37 elections in 16 countries under proportional representation. We show that candidate-centred campaigning is more prevalent in open list systems, but that this institutional effect is not uniform. Candidates from leftleaning parties are more party-centred, and the personalising effect of open lists is weaker among them than among candidates from right leaning parties. These findings show that the consequences of electoral reform depend on the normative and strategic contexts in which parties operate.

articles.title: Examining US–China strategic competition: The case of China’s global initiatives at the United Nations Secretariat
articles.abstract: The well-reported multilateral rise of the People’s Republic of China (PRC or China) is presumed to challenge US leadership in a Western-dominated United Nations (UN) system. Among China’s many multilateral contributions are its advance of “Global Initiatives,” which China frames as “global public goods.” This paper applies sociological interpretations of power, specifically the Barnett & Duvall 2005 typology, to investigate the different strategies used by China to seed three of these Global Initiatives within and upon the UN Secretariat: the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, and the Global Civilization Initiative. While these Global Initiatives are still in their infancy, the research finds variation in how China is approaching each Initiative within the UN system and that these “global public goods” are sites of US–China strategic competition. The research draws from primary and secondary sources produced by PRC and UN elites and foreign policy researchers, and is supplemented by interviews of officials of the PRC, the United States, and the United Nations.

articles.title: From Bombay Street to Ballymena: The repertoires of sectarian violence and 21st-century racism
articles.authors: José A. Gutiérrez, Matthew Whiting, Shannon Doherty
articles.abstract: During June 2025, Ballymena was the epicentre of some of the most serious riots witnessed recently in Northern Ireland. For many days, mobs attacked migrants’ properties and battled the police. These riots soon extended to other areas, the youths involved in the rioting coming overwhelmingly from working-class Loyalist strongholds. We argue that these riots embodied a familiar repertoire of bottom-up Loyalist, non-lethal violence against civilians, shaped by historical sectarianism. We compare the dynamics of the 1969 Bombay Street burnings and the Ballymena riots, demonstrating the persistence of repertoires of violence anchored in sectarianism but assuming new forms in contemporary racism. Although the target group in each instance is different, the repertoire, technique, performative and symbolic dimensions, and underlying ideology of the violence have many continuities, including an effort to cleanse a territory of people seen as undesirable to assert an identity-based control over it, indicating the depth of Loyalist resolve.

The year is a dropdown menu: Platformed provenance and the viral afterlives of AI-generated retro music
articles.abstract: This article examines how generative AI media becomes believable and shareable when it is packaged as a rediscovered archive and distributed through commercial platforms. Drawing on multi-sited digital ethnography, targeted platform walkthroughs, and cross-platform trace analysis of a viral “lost song” circulating in Italy in 2025, I show how listeners in this case mobilized sonic cues and platform metadata, including release dates and credits, as practical evidence. I use metadata realism to describe everyday reliance on database fields as documentary testimony, and provenance play for situated practices of verification and narration through which people negotiate synthetic pasts. After public debunking, circulation continued through humorous and artistic reframings, while verification itself became part of the artifact’s social life. The analysis foregrounds platformed provenance and considers what the case implies for synthetic media governance and content credentials.

articles.title: Ambivalent algorithms, fragile connectedness: How algorithm awareness facets shape responsiveness and insensitivity on TikTok
articles.abstract: This study examines how distinct facets of algorithm awareness are associated with perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR), perceived algorithm insensitivity (PAI), and social connectedness on TikTok. I draw on the algorithm responsiveness process and also treat algorithm awareness as four distinct dimensions (content filtering, automated decision‑making, human–algorithm interplay (HAI), ethical concerns) to examine how each dimension is differentially associated with PAR and PAI and, in turn, with feelings of inclusion and belonging. Using survey data from 305 TikTok users and structural equation modeling, I show that user‑agency‑oriented dimensions, particularly filtering and HAI, are indirectly associated with connectedness via higher responsiveness and lower insensitivity. By contrast, automation operates as an ambivalent structure: it boosts responsiveness yet is negatively associated with connectedness, marking a boundary condition for personalization. Platforms should pair automation disclosures with clearer user recourse, traceable feedback, and human review in high-stakes contexts.

articles.title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
articles.authors: Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton
articles.abstract: This paper explores the perception of social currency as a distinct value within local news consumption among audiences. Social currency refers to the value individuals derive from engaging with and sharing news content within their social networks, allowing them to connect, express identity and signal awareness. Drawing on a large-scale mixed-methods study of local news audiences in Australia (survey: n = 7919; interviews and focus groups: n = 84), this study operationalised key dimensions of social currency using factor analysis. The findings confirm that social currency is a separate and measurable construct, distinct from traditional news motivations. It is significantly higher among younger people, men, urban residents and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, reflecting how news consumption intersects with social interaction, identity expression and symbolic practices of everyday life.

articles.title: Echoes of the public: Public opinion and subnational compliance with European environmental directives
articles.abstract: This study investigates whether public opinion shapes compliance with European environmental directives. Drawing on an original dataset of subnational infringements from 2005 to 2018 across 319 subnational authorities in 20 member states, the analysis links variation in public opinion to compliance using mixed-effects logistic regression models. The results show that subnational public opinion does not exert an independent effect on the likelihood of infringement. Instead, national environmental attitudes emerge as consistently relevant for subnational compliance, with subnational authorities in member states that are less supportive of environmental protection significantly more likely to infringe European Union legislation. Subnational environmental attitudes matter where national environmental support is weak. These findings demonstrate that responsiveness in multilevel governance is conditional upon the interaction between national and subnational public opinion.

articles.title: Administrative Burden and the Access–Fraud Trade‐Off
articles.abstract: Administrative burden represents political choices embedded in policy design that affect how people perceive and experience government. While policymakers frequently invoke fraud prevention to justify imposing burdens in welfare programs, this rhetoric embodies an unacknowledged normative judgment about the relative costs of fraud and abuse versus program exclusion for eligible beneficiaries. This study quantifies this access–fraud trade‐off in means‐tested social welfare programs through a contingent valuation experiment ( N = 2250). We find that respondents were willing to accept approximately 192 ineligible recipients receiving benefits in exchange for 1000 eligible beneficiaries not being excluded due to administrative burdens. While we find no direct evidence that psychological distance (i.e., randomized exposure to “welfare” vs. specific programs) affects this trade‐off across the full sample, political affiliation is a significant moderator in our exploratory analysis. Unlike Democrats/Independents, Republicans demonstrate substantially lower tolerance for potential fraud when evaluating abstract “welfare” compared to specific programs like unemployment insurance. Experience with means‐tested welfare programs, which reduces psychological distance, has a similar moderating effect. These findings extend construal level theory to administrative burden preferences and contribute to the policy implementation literature by quantifying the access–fraud trade‐off—a metric largely absent from academic and policy discussions despite its importance for program legitimacy.

articles.title: The Heterogeneous Impact of Short-Time Work: From Saved Jobs to Windfall Effects,
articles.authors: Pierre Cahuc, Francis Kramarz, Sandra Nevoux, Nathan Vieira
articles.abstract: This paper investigates the adoption of short-time work by firms and their participating employees. We present a model showing that short-time work can preserve jobs in firms facing severe negative revenue shocks, but not in less affected firms, where hours are reduced without preventing layoffs. Using data from all French establishments during the 2008-2009 Great Recession, we find that short-time work helped save jobs and increased hours worked in firms hit by significant revenue losses, facilitating a faster post-recession recovery. We also identify substantial windfall effects, which raise the policy’s cost per job saved. Nonetheless, short-time work is likely more cost-effective at preserving employment than wage subsidies, potentially resulting in a net negative cost to public finances.

articles.title: Polygyny and the Economic Determinants of Family Formation in Sub-Saharan Africa,
articles.abstract: Social norms and formal institutions governing marriage markets vary widely across societies. This paper examines how polygyny norms in Sub-Saharan Africa shape marriage market responses to aggregate economic shocks and their resulting welfare implications. Unlike monogamous markets, polygynous markets feature intense competition for brides between young bachelors and older married men seeking a second (junior) wife. I show, both theoretically and empirically, that the latter group is more responsive than the former to aggregate income shocks in areas where the shadow price of marrying a junior wife is low. This difference in sensitivity leads to distinct equilibrium outcomes: adverse shocks increase the incidence of child marriage in monogamous areas but have no detectable effect in polygynous areas. These divergent equilibrium outcomes generate stark differences in the long-term effects of such shocks on female education, literacy, and the utilization of preventive care services.

articles.title: Exclusive Secrets,
articles.authors: David Angenendt, Giacomo Calzolari, Alireza Naghavi
articles.abstract: We investigate the effects of trade secret (TS) protection on supplier exclusivity in vertical industrial relations. We show that manufacturers limit their suppliers’ buyer networks under weak TS protection to safeguard sensitive information while encouraging supplier investment. Using worldwide automotive parts contracts data, we find that weak TS protection constrains suppliers to serve only a few Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), sometimes leading to exclusivity, especially for parts with intermediate relationship-specificity. This association strengthens with greater OEM bargaining power, aligning with theoretical insights. We validate these findings by examining supplier attributes, including size, cartel involvement, and ownership structure. F23, O34, L14, L24, L62

articles.title: Philanthropic Foundations in Environmental Governance
articles.authors: Rebecca L. Gruby, Michele M. Betsill, Xavier Basurto, Jeffrey E. Blackwatters, Ash Enrici, Dustin Garrick, Agni Kalfagianni, Daniel C. Miller, Anne Monier
articles.abstract: This review examines the involvement of philanthropic foundations in environmental governance. Foundation funding for environmental issues has surged in recent years, elevating the role of philanthropic actors in shaping environmental agendas, policies, organizations, and discourses globally. Foundations remain understudied in the literature on multi-actor environmental governance, however, with implications for both research and practice. Increased research attention to foundations as environmental governance actors is especially needed amid growth in green giving, shrinking public environmental funding, and intensifying scrutiny of the philanthropic sector. The review thus outlines trends in funding flows from foundations for environmental issues, conceptualizes foundations as environmental governance actors, highlights existing research on foundations’ environmental governance roles and legitimacy, and addresses methodological challenges for research on philanthropy. We conclude with a call to action for increased research and engagement between environmental governance scholars and philanthropic foundations to both inform environmental philanthropy as a field of practice and enhance environmental governance scholarship.

articles.title: Urban Informality and Climate Change: Precarity, Governance, and Pathways to Resilience
articles.authors: David Corbett, Pourya Salehi, Debra C. Roberts, Marcus Foth, Maryke van Staden, Aloke Barnwal, Asad Asadzadeh
articles.abstract: Climate change is worsening long-standing inequalities for people living and working in cities’ informal systems, where exposure to heat, flooding, and other hazards intersects with insecure land rights, weak infrastructure, and unstable livelihoods. Using an informality-first approach, this review considers informal housing, economies, and governance not as leftover categories but as essential modes of urbanization and citizenship that define who is protected from climate risk. We review recent research on climate impacts, daily and community-based adaptation, and nature-based solutions in informal settings and combine this with long-standing debates on informality, marginality, and urban governance. The evidence shows that climate change acts as a threat multiplier: It adds stress to informal systems due to climate-induced migration to cities; worsens structural insecurity; and can turn well-meaning adaptation into maladaptation through eviction, green-led displacement, and shifting adaptation burdens onto already overburdened residents. The review suggests that resilience in informal settlements relies less on technical fixes and more on governance structures that recognize informal systems, share authority, and institutionalize coproduction across local, regional, and national levels. Middle-out governance and multilevel governance are crucial for aligning top-down resources with bottom-up knowledge and claims to the city. Ultimately, climate adaptation will either reinforce or challenge urban inequality, depending on whether it treats informality as a core, rather than a peripheral, part of modern urban life.

articles.title: Family Formation and Residential Mobility: How Do Fertility and Mobility Intentions Influence Residential Mobility?
articles.authors: Sarah Christison, Hill Kulu, Katherine Keenan, Francesca Fiori
articles.abstract: In this study, we examine the association between fertility and mobility intentions, and residential mobility. Existing literature suggests a link between family formation and residential moves. However, these studies have not explored the interaction between fertility intentions and mobility intentions, or how they interact with micro‐level, individual factors such as current family size and housing context, or temporal effects that can serve as proxies for macro‐level contextual factors, such as changes in the housing market or economy. Utilising harmonised data from the British Household Panel Survey and the UK Household Longitudinal Survey, and employing event history analysis techniques, we investigate the interaction between the two life course domains of fertility and residential mobility. We consider not only how jointly held intentions influence the likelihood of a residential relocation, but also how the influence of these intentions varies across population subgroups and over time, particularly focusing on the effect of the 2008 financial crisis. We find that intending to have a(nother) child does increase the likelihood of a residential move; however, this association varies based on individual‐level characteristics and contextual factors. Intentions to have a child in the future are only positively associated with residential mobility for women intending a higher‐order birth and those who are married. Moreover, the positive association between fertility intentions and residential moves for mothers was observed only prior to the 2008 financial crisis. The financial crisis also affected the relationship between mobility intentions and the likelihood of a move, with individuals less likely to realise their mobility intentions following the financial crash and subsequent recession. This temporal effect suggests that people may be more limited in their ability to fulfil their mobility intentions under challenging economic conditions and unfavourable housing markets.

articles.title: Migration Security and Regional Socio‐Economic Resilience in Ukraine: Dynamics, Differentiation and Implications
articles.authors: Vitaliy Krupin, Olha Mulska, Ihor Baranyak, Marta Kunytska‐Ilyash
articles.abstract: Ukraine presents a critical case for understanding how migration processes shape regional socio‐economic resilience, yet no regionally explicit framework has previously linked internal and external migration security to territorial differentiation across its oblasts. This article addresses that gap by developing a composite regional indicator integrating internal and external migration security dimensions, applied to 24 oblasts over 2010–2021, that captures both the scale and directional influence of migration on regional resilience. Results reveal substantial differentiation that does not follow conventional macro‐regional lines: mean values range from 0.826 in Kyiv oblast to 0.421 in Zakarpattia, yet western and eastern industrial oblasts differ little as groups (0.606 and 0.630) relative to the spread within each, with Chernivtsi, a western border oblast, ranking second nationally and Ternopil, a western agrarian oblast, ninth. Level and temporal stability prove largely independent: the most volatile region, Kharkiv, moved repeatedly between the top and the bottom of the national distribution, while cross‐regional dispersion widened over the period, indicating divergence rather than uniform decline. Extended to 2022–2024, a separate contextual analysis drawing on aggregate official, IOM and UNHCR data examines how far this pre‐war geography corresponds to the uneven consequences of wartime displacement, with 10.5 million people having fled Ukraine and 3.7 million internally displaced by August 2024; the correspondence is partial, and this extension is interpretive rather than a formal causal test. The framework provides both a replicable measurement tool and an empirical baseline for post‐war regional recovery analysis.

articles.title: Marital Status, Cohabitation and Intentions of Workers to Move to Less Developed Areas
articles.authors: Yuyao Liu, Linghan Ge, Chenxiao Wang, Eric Fong
articles.abstract: While migration for ‘love in destinations’ has gained attention, the link between partnerships, beyond the married‐unmarried dichotomy, in home societies and migration intentions remains underexplored. Meanwhile, economies in the Global South are becoming attractive for talent, yet little is known about intentions of workers to migrate within this region. This study analyzes how marital status and cohabitation relate to Hong Kong workers’ intentions to move to less developed Mainland Chinese cities. Using survey data, it compares short‐term (within 5 years) and long‐term migration intentions across single, partnered non‐cohabiting, cohabiting and married workers. Short‐term intentions are higher among married or cohabiting men than single men. Long‐term intentions are stronger among married than single women. Family presence moderates these associations. Workers with non‐cohabitating partners do not differ from single counterparts. Findings highlighted the role of partnerships and living arrangements on migration intentions and contributed novel insights for theorizing educated migration.

Violence Against Feminist Advocates: Political Violence and Anti-Gender Politics
articles.abstract: Research on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) and research on violence against women activists have made crucial contributions by conceptualizing violence as a gendered phenomenon that targets women in response to their political participation. In these approaches, violence operates as a mechanism to discipline, silence, or expel women from political and public life. Alongside these developments, a growing body of scholarship has examined anti-gender politics as a structured and transnational political project, paying particular attention to its actors, discourses, and strategies.

articles.title: VAWIP in a State-Monopolized Political Field: The Case of Chinese Feminist Activism
articles.abstract: The literature on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) implicitly treats such violence as boundary enforcement: a political field already exists; the violence women encounter marks the edge they are not permitted to cross; and the state stands as the guarantor of protection and redress under the rule of law, whether or not it delivers (Krook 2020; Krook and Restrepo Sanín2016). In high-capacity authoritarian states like China (Johnston 2019), the premise of this framing does not hold. The political field itself is monopolized and policed by the state, which determines what counts as politics, who is recognized as a legitimate political subject, and what forms of political action are permitted.

articles.title: Compliant Women, Constitutive Violence: Rethinking the VAWIP Counterfactual
articles.abstract: The literature on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) has made substantial contributions to understanding how gender shapes political exclusion. Foundational work by Krook and Restrepo Sanín (2016; 2020) defined VAWIP as a form of hate crime and as systematic backlash against women’s entry into political life. This conceptual scaffolding informs Krook’s (2022) subsequent attention to semiotic and symbolic harm, extending the VAWIP framework beyond physical violence to encompass the representational strategies through which female politicians are delegitimized. Bjarnegård and Zetterberg’s (2023) edited volume extends the framework further, recognizing that gender-based political violence operates across a broader range of contexts and along a “psychological-physical continuum” (7) that is neither temporally nor institutionally confined to election cycles or legislative chambers.

articles.title: Explaining Violence Against Feminist Activists and Women Human Rights Defenders
articles.abstract: On March 2, 2026, Iraqi feminist activist Yanar Mohammed was assassinated by armed militants at her home in Baghdad. Since founding the Organization of Women’s Freedom in Iraq (OWFI) in 2004, Mohammed had been repeatedly targeted by anti-rights and fundamentalist forces seeking to repress her advocacy for women’s rights. She was a pioneer in building feminist infrastructure to support women and girls fleeing violence, while also publicly challenging the U.S.-led war, militarization, and patriarchal governance.

articles.title: Triadic Victimization in Violence Against Women in Politics: Repairing Justice and Restoring Democracy in Japan
articles.abstract: Violence against women in politics (VAWIP) is a widespread phenomenon that deters women from fully engaging with political activities, particularly from running for office. Not only office seekers but also a broader range of women actors, such as journalists, human rights defenders, and civil servants, experience sexual harassment and assault perpetrated by political actors (Krook 2020). While much of the literature on violence against women in politics focuses on the incidence of such violence and policy solutions, this article broadens the analytical scope to theorize how institutional responses to redress harms may not resolve but instead exacerbate violence through further layers of victimization.

articles.title: Corruption and Uneven Development: Why Anti‐Corruption Fails in the EU 's Most Vulnerable Regions
articles.authors: Ina Kubbe, Stoyan Panov, Wisnu Setiadi Nugroho, Fatih Kırşanlı
articles.abstract: This article challenges the assumption that legal harmonization within the European Union ensures effective anti‐corruption governance. Despite EU‐compliant frameworks, institutional integrity remains highly uneven across subnational territories. We introduce the Regional Integrity Framework (RIF), a diagnostic approach that integrates citizen perceptions, procurement indicators, and enforcement activation measures to capture regional integrity performance. The analysis suggests that formal convergence can conceal functional divergence, as peripheral regions often exhibit weaker administrative capacity, limited oversight, and uneven institutional activation. A mixed‐methods application that combines panel analysis with an illustrative comparison of Sofia and Vidin, Bulgaria, demonstrates how the RIF can diagnose territorial integrity gaps within a shared legal framework. Conceptually, the study reframes anti‐corruption as a territorially embedded problem of institutional activation; methodologically, it offers a transferable framework for identifying enforcement asymmetries and governance disparities in multi‐level systems.

articles.title: De‐Risking or Dividing? Jurisdictional Carbon Markets and the Politics of Risk Management
articles.abstract: Jurisdictional approaches under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement are rapidly shaping global carbon markets. By linking emissions mitigation activities to state action and broader policy frameworks, these approaches are often presented as a way to address some of the integrity and ethical concerns associated with project‐based carbon crediting. Yet the risk of not delivering committed credit volumes persists regardless of scale, governance actor, or institutional structure. To manage this credit delivery risk, financial products such as carbon insurance are increasingly viewed as critical. This paper argues that private performance insurance should not be understood as a neutral technical fix. While it may help manage some delivery risks, it can also create new forms of inequity by making coverage more costly, restrictive, or unavailable for jurisdictions deemed “higher risk”. These jurisdictions may also be those most in need of climate finance. Private insurance should therefore be considered only as part of a broader risk management architecture that includes public or hybrid insurance mechanisms, carbon buffers, temporary crediting, and direct investment in risk reduction. Considered policy design is essential to ensure Article 6.2 initiatives and jurisdictional carbon markets promote inclusive, sustainable, and effective climate outcomes. articles.title: When habit prevails: a causal test of policy feedback theory using a pension reform
articles.authors: Michael Ganslmeier, Margaryta Klymak, Tim Vlandas
articles.abstract: Elderly voters are a growing, politically powerful electoral bloc, and their pensions often constitute the largest component of welfare state. We know that cuts can provoke electoral backlash, but it is less clear whether benefit expansions mobilize retirees. Some policy feedback theories predict increased participation following material gains, but recent evidence on policy expansions is mixed. While income and political participation appear correlated among the elderly, habit formation theory implies that older voters may be a least likely case for benefit expansion leading to mobilization. Leveraging a pension reform in Illinois that increased benefits by 36% for retirees, a regression discontinuity design on administrative data covering 93,000 public employees across twelve elections shows no turnout effect, even among low-income groups.

articles.title: Just to be clear? Strategic vagueness of the European Parliament in EU policy negotiations
articles.authors: Aleksandra Khokhlova, Nikoleta Yordanova, Anastasia Ershova
articles.abstract: Vague legislative language can facilitate law adoption and implementation but reduce policy effectiveness and application uniformity. So, when do legislators employ it? Building on policymaking and responsiveness theories, we argue that legislators use vague language to overcome institutional conflict and public opinion constraints but avoid it when they seek to assert their positions in legislative output and policy outcomes. Empirically, we study the conditions under which the European Parliament (EP) introduces vague amendments to European Union (EU) legislative proposals using dictionary-based content analysis of EU legislative negotiations between 2009 and 2019. The results show that EP sticks to more concrete positions when inter-institutional conflict threatens its policy goals but employs vagueness to maintain a broad appeal and avoid public backlash given public opinion divisions and contentiousness. These results add to our knowledge of legal text formulation, EU law making, and EP representation.

articles.title: Echoes of conflict: quantifying redundancy in fatality time series
articles.abstract: Do wars follow predictable patterns, or are they chaotic and inherently unpredictable? We explore this question by quantifying temporal redundancy—how often similar patterns recur—in conflict-related fatalities. Using entropy-based analysis—a measure of randomness—and Dynamic Time Warping, we compare conflict dynamics with other complex systems such as seismology and finance. Our findings reveal that the dynamics of fatalities within conflicts exhibit high levels of entropy: they are largely unpredictable. Conflicts generally display higher entropy than climate or earthquake data, which highlights the challenges of predictive modeling. Moreover, conflict patterns are not region- or decade-specific, which suggests a degree of universality. Our framework distinguishes stable from chaotic phases in conflict dynamics and clarifies where forecasting is feasible.

articles.title: High accuracy with low costs: the pretrain-finetune paradigm for classification with transformer-based language models
articles.abstract: Political science increasingly uses text classification to gauge subtle concepts such as toxicity or anger. Traditional methods treat words in isolation, overlooking the contextual dynamics where meaning resides. Transformer-based language models address these limitations but remain underutilized, especially among applied scholars, partly due to misconceptions about their mechanisms and computational requirements. This article bridges this gap by offering an accessible explication of the pretrain-finetune paradigm, focusing on underlying mechanisms and their potential to improve political text analysis by harnessing models trained on extensive datasets while requiring modest labeled data and computational resources. I demonstrate the approach by identifying toxic language in conversation threads following U.S. Senators’ tweets and provide an online tutorial to support nontechnical scholars in adopting the methodology.

articles.title: Does preference intensity matter? Reexamining policy representation in the American states
articles.authors: Zachary Peskowitz, Eddy S. F. Yeung
articles.abstract: Preference intensity may play an important role in shaping mass political behavior, yet existing empirical scholarship on representation typically relies on survey measures that capture public opinion in terms of preference directionality without intensity. We use a variety of measures—not only the standard Likert and “most important policy” items but also the quadratic voting method—to reassess responsiveness and congruence of a diverse set of American state policies that vary in issue areas and salience. Across multiple novel measures of individual policy preferences, we consistently find that state-level preference intensity does not reliably predict actual policy outcomes. We contribute new evidence that the lack of policy representation in the American states remains—even if preference intensity is systematically integrated into the empirical analysis.

articles.title: Shared Discrimination’s Effect on Solidarity between People of Color Is Uniform Across Major Racial, Political, and Social Differences
articles.authors: Kasheena Rogbeer, Emily Ortiz, Efrén Pérez
articles.abstract: Solidarity between people of color (PoC) is key to understanding multiracial coalition-building in the United States. However, limited statistical power has constrained research on whether shared discrimination’s effect on solidarity is reliably moderated by differences in race, political orientation, and social background, which structure the internal diversity of racially stigmatized subgroups within the mega-category, PoC. We report a preregistered meta-analysis of eight published experiments ( N = 5,813), which used a common design to test shared discrimination’s effects among Black Americans, Asian Americans, Latinos, and Middle Eastern and North African individuals. Despite known heterogeneity in these group’s social and political attitudes, we find that shared discrimination’s effect on solidarity is statistically uniform across race/ethnicity, partisanship, ideology, nativity, education, gender, and age. These results indicate that shared discrimination appeals broadly and reliably activate solidarity across diverse PoC subgroups, further affirming this psychological mechanism’s crucial role in fostering robust multiracial coalitions.

articles.title: Digital Public Mental Health: a dataset for monitoring mental health in Brazil
articles.authors: Gabriel Souto, Marcel Pedroso, Raquel de Souza Martins, Rebecca Salles, Matheus Miloski, Carmen Corrêa Bonifácio, Ariane Camilo Pinheiro Alves, Carlos Leonardo Souza Cardoso, Carolina C. Carvalho, Ricardo A. D. Oliveira, Flavio Kapczinski, Ives C. Passos, Jefferson da Costa Lima, Raquel B. De Boni
articles.abstract: The scarcity of primary data and challenges in analyzing secondary data hinder comprehensive mental health monitoring and the development of evidence-based policies. In Brazil, although multiple health information systems capture critical mental health data, these systems lack integration, robust analysis, and systematic presentation of mental health indicators. This study introduces the Digital Public Mental Health Dataset, a comprehensive, transparent, and reproducible data resource that consolidates data from existing Brazilian health information systems. This dataset enables detailed tracking of mental health indicators, supports future research, and informs public health interventions to address mental health disparities.

articles.title: Far-right music events, protests, and violence: a county-level dataset for Germany, 2013–2024
articles.abstract: Far-right activism materializes in music events, marches, and violence. Yet, the empirical links between these types of activism remain unclear. Quantifying these manifestations is difficult because of fragmented reporting and inconsistent geocoding at the local level. We introduce the Far-Right Activism (FARAC) dataset, a panel (2013–2024) that aggregates German federal parliamentary inquiries and civil society records at the county level. The dataset addresses the problem of regional assignment by standardizing all event records in accordance with 2024 administrative boundaries. This harmonized structure permits the first systematic, local-level comparison of far-right activism. It uses standard administrative identifiers, enabling direct integration with electoral results, sociodemographic indicators, and other county-level datasets.

articles.title: What does the public know about their State’s abortion laws in the post-Dobbs era?
articles.authors: Marisa Abrajano, Marianna Garcia, Aaron Pope, Robert Vidigal, Jonathan Nagler
articles.abstract: Following the Dobbs decision in the U.S., there were widespread reports of misinformation regarding the ruling. Many Americans may therefore have faced uncertainty about abortion laws in their state, and Latinos—approximately 40% of whom are foreign-born—may be particularly vulnerable due to limited familiarity with the U.S. political system. To better understand awareness of state abortion policies, we fielded a national online panel survey containing large samples of Latinos ( N = 2326) and non-Hispanic whites ( N = 769). We find that Latinos were 6 percentage points less likely to correctly identify their state’s abortion law relative to white Americans and were 10.7 percentage points more likely to overestimate the strictness of those laws, even when controlling for demographic, religious, and political covariates. Foreign-born Latinos were also 19.5 percentage points more likely to overestimate the strictness of their state’s abortion law compared to their U.S.-born counterparts. These findings contribute to our understanding of differential learning following sudden policy change and highlight significant knowledge gaps that may affect whether individuals seek abortion care if they misunderstand the legal status in their state. Such gaps may have downstream consequences for health care access and economic inequality.

articles.title: Humilitainment 2.0: Platformed Crime Entertainment and Digital Carcerality on YouTube
articles.abstract: Reality-based crime television has long shaped public understandings of policing, crime, and punishment by turning law enforcement encounters into consumable spectacle. As these narratives migrate into engagement-driven platform infrastructures, where recommendation systems and interactive features reshape how policing media is packaged, encountered, and monetized, their cultural impact is reconfigured. This article examines COPSTV, the official YouTube continuation of COPS , as platformed crime entertainment structured for visibility and circulation. Drawing on a thematic analysis of 200 highly viewed COPSTV videos, I identify three interrelated patterns: the packaging of policing encounters for visibility through sensationalized titles, rapid escalation, and spectacle-oriented narrative sequencing; recurring representations that glorify law enforcement, individualize criminality, criminalize mental health crises, and normalize police violence; and the conversion of public humiliation into a platformed strategy of engagement. I argue that YouTube’s recommendation infrastructure may contribute to the amplification of punitive narratives by increasing the visibility of highly engaging policing content, positioning viewers for participatory judgment while crowding out structural critique. Situating COPSTV within scholarship on platform governance, media convergence, and digital carcerality, the article shows how platform dynamics render coercion and degradation highly visible, clickable, and economically self-reinforcing.

articles.title: Antecedents of Disclosure: What Transparency Measures Social Media Users in the United States Want From Paid Political Influencers
articles.authors: Martin J. Riedl, Benjamin D. Horne, Matthew J. A. Craig, Michael R. Kotowski, Catherine A. Luther
articles.abstract: At the heels of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, public attention turned to the role social media influencers played in Donald J. Trump’s decisive win. In the United States, unlike influencers promoting commercial brands, political influencers – that is, social media influencers who associate themselves with political causes – are not required to disclose whether they got paid in exchange for promoting a political organization, party, or campaign. Through a survey of U.S. social media users ( n = 906), this study explores people’s attitudes toward paid political influencer disclosure. We find that political partisanship impacts support for disclosure: being more conservative is connected to lessened support for disclosure, yet disclosure is of strong bipartisan concern regardless. Our study documents that social media users who care for authenticity – a core currency in influencer ecosystems running on parasocial relationships – also exhibit higher support for disclosure. Yet, at the same time, caveating this empirical relationship between authenticity and disclosure, we also found that those who consumed more political influencer content exhibited lower support for disclosure, pinpointing the normalization of a digital ecology replete with sponsored content. Our study has implications for the broader political communication ecology: As transparency for paid political influencer activities emerges as a topic of public concern, platforms and regulators should advance efforts that provide disclosure about paid political influencer activities to social media users.

articles.title: Social Robots and the Dialectics of Presence and Absence
articles.authors: Autumn Edwards, Chad Edwards, Bryan Abendschein
articles.abstract: Social robots function as embodied social media, structuring interaction by simultaneously acting as social agents and mediating technologies. This study examines how 103 young adult participants engaged with zoomorphic social robots in initial encounters, revealing dialectical tensions between presence and absence, connection and disconnection, and realism and artificiality. Drawing from relational dialectics theory (RDT) and semiotics, we frame social robots within a plural communication ontology—operating both as communicative partners and as structuring media that regulate relational expectations. Findings indicate that while social robots facilitate engagement, their enacted affordances also constrain interaction, exposing the limits of artificial presence. Like social media platforms, these robots curate sociality, fostering immersion while highlighting mediation. By conceptualizing social robots as communicative infrastructures, this study advances research on human–machine communication and technological mediation, illustrating how social robots shape social connection through structured engagement and interactive constraints.

articles.title: “Turns Out My Paternal Grandmother has 16% Native Blood”: Racialized DNA, Race Destabilization, and Digital Race-(re)making on Social Media
articles.abstract: This study explores an online phenomenon that we conceptualize as “digital race (re)-making.” In the context of genetic ancestry test discourses, we found digital race (re)-making a sequential four-stage race-making process where users (a) authenticate their previously identified racial identity, (b) destabilize the previous race by incorporating DNA test results, (c) negotiate potential conflict between their previous racial identity and the DNA-inferred race, and (d) utilize social media to affirm and contest their negotiation. Employing multi-round discourse analysis on 466 self-disclosing narratives on the subreddit r/23andMe, we explore the semiotics, strategies, and signifiers that users deployed to discursively disrupt their previously identified racial identity and to create and compose their newly constructed racial identity under the premise of genetic race. By surfacing such a new online racial formation process, we argue that digital platforms actively shape the ways race is re-constructed, re-contested, and re-configured. We also discuss how such a process repudiates the classical identity formation model and how it extends racial socialization theory to the digital enclaves, and how such self-discovery comes with emotional cost.

articles.title: Whose Team Are You On? Evaluating Public Response to Native American Policy Priorities
articles.abstract: Native American advocates and Tribal Nations have fought for decades against the use of Native imagery in sports mascots. In recent years, national sports franchises, colleges, and states have started responding to these demands by changing team names and iconography. As these policy changes have been framed as racial equity initiatives rather than matters of Native sovereignty, some professional teams continue to use Native imagery, and many states remain entrenched in debates over legislative mandates to remove such imagery from K-12 school sports. This project uses data from two survey experiments to examine how predominantly White fan bases respond to requests from tribal leaders, White allies, and partisan officials to support tribal policy priorities. Results indicate that the racial identity of the messenger significantly influences support for changing mascot practices, with Native messengers eliciting the strongest positive shifts in opinion.

Digital twins are funhouse mirrors: Five systematic distortions
articles.authors: Tianyi Peng, Melanie Brucks, George Gui, Daniel J. Merlau, Grace Jiarui Fan, Malek Ben Sliman, Eric J. Johnson, Abdullah Althenayyan, Silvia Bellezza, Dante Donati, Hortense Fong, Elizabeth Friedman, Ariana Guevara, Mohamed Hussein, Kinshuk Jerath, Bruce Kogut, Akshit Kumar, Kristen Lane, Hannah Li, Vicki Morwitz, Oded Netzer, Patryk Perkowski, Olivier Toubia
articles.abstract: Scientists and practitioners are aggressively moving to deploy digital twins—large language model (LLM)-based models of individuals—across social science and policy research. We conducted 19 preregistered studies with 164 diverse outcomes (e.g., attitudes toward hiring algorithms and intention to share misinformation) and compared human responses with those of their digital twins (trained on each person’s previous answers to more than 500 questions). We establish an empirical benchmark for digital twin performance: Digital twins’ answers are only modestly more accurate than those from the (homogeneous) base LLM and correlate weakly with human responses (average correlation coefficient of 0.20). To guide future development, we document five ways in which digital twins distort human behavior: (i) insufficient individuation, (ii) stereotyping, (iii) representation bias, (iv) ideological biases, and (v) hyper-rationality. We make our full dataset and code public as a standardized testbed. Our results caution against premature deployment while laying the groundwork for the transparent, replicable, and iterative science necessary for responsible deployment of digital twins.
